I started out in 'live hang'

Live birds come in on a conveyor belt, dropped out of cages unloaded from trucks. Done in the dark so the birds stay calm. Blacklight is the only light there. Goal: hang 80+ birds a minute. Pick em up by the legs, drop em in the shackles, facing the right way (ass facing you.) Wrong way birds have a hard time on the killroom and pickers. Squawking, kicking, flapping, crowing, SHITTING birds, and you gotta hang them like your ass is on fire. The great part about this area is when you get shit on in the head or face, you HEAR it hitting you like a fart noise. Mostly hispanics in this area, and they haul ass every day. You wear 3 layers of protection from shit, including goggles and particle mask, and you still smell like ass when you get home. THIS was the disgusting area.

Next birds go to the kill room. Waterbath, high voltage to knock them out, then some wheels and bars guide the necks to the killblade. right after that is the last resort, one person standing there all day with a knife catching any birds that missed the blade. His job was to cut throats all day.

Then to the blanching/picking. Alternating temperature water baths to loosen the birds up for picking. Then the pickers (for removing feathers.) Rows of machines did all this without much help. at the end of the pick room was the head puller. i was fascinated by this for some reason. just a couple bars shaped into a V that tipped downward, as the birds went by. heads dropped neatly into a tray in the floor that washed into different trucks for assorted uses.

Next is evisceration. The bird line swaps the birds off to another line with stainless shackles to prep for guts. One machine drills out the asshole, then lays it to the side. Next machine is kinda like a spoon-shape wire structure that enters against the inside of the chest, and scoops the guts out. Next is hand pulling, inspection, and trim. Each bird must be inspected by the USDA, and they have 2 seconds to look at each bird. If you're a puller, you have 2 seconds to reach in, clear the tendons and membranes from the carcass, lay the guts to the right, and leave the flaps open. USDA does their look into the bird, then drops the guts. If anything's bad or needs trim, USDA calls it, and the trimmer acts accordingly, while also looking for feet.

From there, they'll be dumped off their shackles into a chiller tank (birds cut easier when they're closer to freezing.) Then dumped out onto a table to be rehung by hand, then on to an automatic halve, then quarter the rear. Everything from this point on is fucking COLD work.

Top half of the bird goes to the cone line, where they're stripped. Production line-style here. 12 different operations to be done, and you do 1 all day. The resulting parts go to marinade, to soak for whatever period.

Next room is flash-freeze and packaging. fill the bag, weigh the bag, put it on the line.

As far as cleaning goes, power washing is the only way to go. At lunch time the whole place got a serious washdown.

TL:DR; Pretty disgusting, depending on where you worked. power washer
